---
title: "Output Formats"
---

Gridwell renders the table IR to 11 output formats, split into text (returns a string) and
binary (returns bytes). Which styling features each Tier-1 writer (HTML, LaTeX, Typst,
RTF, DOCX, XLSX) actually expresses is measured, not claimed: see the
[Feature Matrix](feature-matrix.qmd). Where a format can't express a feature a table
uses (the notes below say which), you can ask for a
[warning](../schema/validation.qmd#warnings) saying where before rendering, and
`gridwell convert` prints one.

Two styles are CSS values that other formats translate:

- `font_family` is a CSS font list, which HTML writes as given. Typst takes the whole
  list as font names; RTF, DOCX, XLSX and PPTX take one font per run, the first name
  in the list. Either way, a generic family becomes a common font (`serif` Times New
  Roman, `sans-serif` Arial, `monospace` Courier New), while generics with no common
  font (`system-ui`, `cursive`, …) and vendor keywords such as `-apple-system` are
  dropped. A list naming no font leaves the format's default font. LaTeX writes only
  monospace families (below); SVG draws in its own font, and ANSI, Pandoc and Quarto
  have no fonts.
- `text_transform` (`uppercase`, `lowercase`, `capitalize`) changes the text itself
  in every format except HTML, where CSS's `text-transform` applies it and the markup
  keeps the text as written. Footnote marks are never transformed.

A style's `font_weight` replaces the weight a format draws by default: `normal` (or
`lighter`) un-bolds column labels, the title or a group label, and a styled run's
weight replaces its cell's, so a `normal` run in a bold cell is not bold. Pandoc and
Quarto have bold (`Strong`) but no way to undo it, and ANSI draws its title and group
labels bold whatever their style. `font_style` works the same way: a `normal` run in
an italic cell, title or note is upright, except in Pandoc and Quarto (`Emph` can't be
undone). Underline and strike-through are different: as in CSS, a run adds them to
its cell's but can't remove them.

## Text Formats

### HTML

- Semantic HTML5 with `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tbody>`, `<tfoot>`
- A fragment for a host page, styled like gt by default: the `<style>` block starts
  with a base stylesheet (system font, the rules above and below the table and around
  the column labels, spanner and row-group rules, the stub's border, footnote and
  source-note sizes, padding), then the table's own styles. The base rules use
  `:where()`, which has zero specificity, so the table's styles and the host page's
  CSS always override them. `base_styles: false` leaves only the table's own styles.
  With `inline_styles` there is no `<style>` block, so no base look either.
- `standalone: true` wraps the fragment in a complete UTF-8 document (doctype, charset,
  viewport, a `<title>` from the table's title), for a file opened directly in a
  browser. Saved `.html` files are fragments unless you pass it.
- Scoped `<style>` block with generated class names
- Optional inline-style mode for email/embedded contexts
- Footnote marks as `<sup>` linked to footer
- Accessibility: the stub is a row header (`<th scope="row">`), and any cell with a
  `scope` is a header cell with that scope; the table takes `aria-label` and
  `aria-describedby` from the config, and `summary` becomes its `<caption>`. A
  browser draws `<th>` bold: the base stylesheet keeps stubs and column labels at
  normal weight, so with `base_styles: false` or `inline_styles` both are bold
- Class names for each structural part (below)

Every structural part has a class, so a stylesheet (the host page's) can target it.
The prefix is `gw` unless the `class_prefix` option changes it, and the classes are
emitted with inline styles too.

| Class | Element | Part |
|---|---|---|
| `gw_container` | `<div>` | Wraps the whole table |
| `gw_title`, `gw_subtitle`, `gw_header_line` | `<div>` | Heading lines above the table |
| `gw_table` | `<table>` | The table |
| `gw_col_labels`, `gw_spanners` | `<tr>` in `<thead>` | Column-label and spanner rows (a head row without a `role` counts as column labels) |
| `gw_col_label`, `gw_spanner` | `<th>` | Column labels; spanner labels (filler cells in a spanner row get no class) |
| `gw_stubhead`, `gw_stub` | `<th>` | Stub column cells in the head and in the body |
| `gw_group_label` | `<td>` | A row group's label |
| `gw_summary`, `gw_grand_summary` | `<tr>` | Summary and grand summary rows |
| `gw_footer`, `gw_footnotes`, `gw_source_notes` | `<div>` | The footer and its two blocks |
| `gw_footnote`, `gw_source_note` | `<p>` | One footnote or source note |
| `gw_footnote_mark` | `<sup>` | A footnote mark, in a cell or before its footnote |

Style classes are added alongside these as `gw_style-<style id>` (e.g.
`class="gw_title gw_style-gw_1"`). That namespace can't meet the part classes, so a
style named `title` styles only what references it, not the title. Generated classes
use a double underscore (`gw__al_left`, `gw__c0`). Style ids are plain names (the
`INVALID_STYLE_ID` rule), and the writer never puts any other id into markup: given
unvalidated IR, it gives such a style a generated `gw__s<n>` class instead.

### LaTeX

- Uses `booktabs` (`\toprule`, `\midrule`, `\bottomrule`); a column spanner is underlined
  with `\cmidrule` over its columns (`\cline` without booktabs)
- `\multicolumn` and `\multirow` for spans
- A table with more than 30 body rows (`longtable_threshold`; `longtable: true` for
  any table) is a `longtable`, which breaks across pages. It starts at the left
  margin, as a tabular does. The title, subtitle and header lines are rows of its
  first head, so a page break can't separate them from the table; the column labels
  head every page; every page ends with the bottom rule; and the footnotes and source
  notes are rows of its last foot, below the last row. These rows span the table
  without widening it. There is no numbered `\caption`. Column widths settle over
  LaTeX runs: compile until LaTeX stops asking to rerun
- Column alignment via `l`, `r`, `c`; a column with a width is a paragraph column
  (`p{…}`, `X`), aligned by `\raggedright`, `\centering` or `\raggedleft` (justified
  only if the column is `justify`), and a cell aligned apart from its column keeps the
  column's width
- Column widths: a fixed width is itself (`px` at 0.75pt). A `%` width is that share
  of the table's width less every column's padding (`2\tabcolsep` each), so shares
  that add up to 100% fill it. `fr` columns share what the others leave, in
  proportion: in a tabular they are `tabularx`'s `X` columns, and the table is
  exactly its width; in a longtable each one's width is worked out from the fixed
  and `%` columns only, so natural-width columns add to the table's width. The
  table's width is `table_width` (default the line, `\linewidth`): it is the width
  that `%` and `fr` columns divide. When `table_width` is set and no column is `fr`,
  the columns without a width are `1fr`, so the table is that wide; otherwise a table
  without `fr` columns keeps its natural width
- Cell fills via `\cellcolor`, text color via `\textcolor`; underline and strike-through via
  `\uline` / `\sout`; sizes via `\fontsize`
- Cell borders: a horizontal edge is a line of its own between two rows (`\omit` cells
  filled with leaders: solid, dashed, dotted or double), so a fill can't paint over it;
  a vertical edge is a `!{\vrule …}` in the cell's `\multicolumn` (a rule is always
  solid, so dashed and dotted sides are drawn solid). A double line's two strokes and
  the gap between them are a third of its width each. Where two cells' borders meet,
  one edge is drawn: the wider, then double, solid, dashed, dotted, then the one above
  or to the left. No packages beyond those below.
- Required packages: `booktabs`, `multirow`, `longtable` (long tables), `tabularx`
  (`fr` columns), `xcolor` with the `table` option, and `ulem` with `normalem`
  (`\usepackage[normalem]{ulem}`, so `\emph` keeps its meaning). `tabularx` reads its
  body as an argument, so raw LaTeX in a table with `fr` columns can't use `\verb`
- Special characters escaped: `& % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \`
- `font_family` is written only for monospace families (`\texttt`, in cells and group
  labels): a named system font needs XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX with `fontspec`, and the
  output also targets pdfLaTeX
- `vertical_align` is not written: a `tabular` row sets its cells on one baseline,
  at its top. A cell spanning rows is a `\multirow`, centered on them
- Lengths are written as given, and TeX holds none above `\maxdimen` (16383.99998pt,
  about 5.75m): a table with a longer one, or with widths that add up to more, doesn't
  compile ("Dimension too large")

### Typst

- Uses Typst's `#table()` function with named parameters
- `table.cell(colspan: N, rowspan: N)` for spans
- Column widths mapped to Typst length values. `%` and `fr` columns divide the
  table's width: a table with `table_width` is a `#block` that wide (a `%` width is a
  share of the container), and its columns without a width are `1fr` when no column
  is; without it, the container's width
- Styles via `table.cell(fill: ...)`, `text(weight: "bold")`
- Fonts via `text(font: ("Georgia", "Times New Roman"))`: the whole list, in order, so
  Typst falls back through it
- Cell borders via `table.cell(stroke: ...)`, solid, dashed or dotted (Typst has no
  double line: a double border is drawn solid)
- Vertical alignment with the cell's horizontal one (`align: left + bottom`)
- The title (bold, 16pt), subtitle and header lines (12pt, gray), group labels (bold on
  light gray) and notes (9pt; source notes gray) take their style's text formatting
  (and a group label its fill) in place of those defaults

### RTF

- Full RTF document with color and font tables; each font in the table is
  classed by its list's generic family (`\froman`, `\fswiss`, `\fmodern`), which a
  reader uses to pick a substitute when the font is missing
- Column spans via `\cellx` boundaries, row spans via `\clvmgf`/`\clvmrg`
- Column widths in twips (1/1440 inch). `%` and `fr` columns divide the table's
  width: `table_width`, else the line, 6in (the document sets no page, so the
  reader's default page decides; RTF's own default, Letter with 1.25in margins, has a
  6in line). When `table_width` is set and no column is `fr`, the columns without a
  width share what the others leave; otherwise each is 1.5in, as is an `fr` column
  the others leave no room for. `em` is 12pt. Every column is at least a twip wide,
  and widths that would add up to more than RTF's largest number (about 38km) are
  scaled down to fit, in proportion
- Cell fills via `\clcbpat`; cell borders via `\clbrdrt`/`\clbrdrl`/`\clbrdrb`/`\clbrdrr`
  (solid, dashed, dotted, double; no table-wide rules)
- Vertical alignment via `\clvertalt`/`\clvertalc`/`\clvertalb`

### SVG

- Standalone SVG image, self-contained (no external dependencies)
- The same default look as HTML (gt's rules, padding, sizes and text color, from one
  shared spec), drawn by gridwell's own layout: the table's styles (fills, bold,
  colors, cell borders and padding) still win
- Text laid out with Roboto's real widths (cells leave room for Arial-compatible
  fallbacks), and every line drawn with `textLength`, so viewers that substitute
  another font keep the layout. librsvg ignores `textLength`, so rsvg-based tools
  (Pandoc/Quarto PDF, R's rsvg) render best with Roboto installed
- Body cells are vertically centered and head cells bottom-aligned, as in HTML, unless
  a style's `vertical_align` says otherwise
- Known differences from HTML: a word too long for a fixed-width column is broken
  inside the column (HTML widens the column), and `max_width` always clamps

### ANSI (Terminal)

- Box-drawing characters for borders (Unicode); rules run unbroken over and under cells
  that span columns
- Footnote marks as Unicode superscripts, in cells and in the notes below
- 24-bit ANSI color sequences
- Column widths computed from content
- Text truncation with ellipsis for overflow
- Saved to a file (`.txt`), it is plain text with no escape codes unless the `color`
  option is set

### Pandoc

- Pandoc JSON AST format (`Table` constructor)
- Supports all inline formatting (Strong, Emph, Superscript, etc.)
- Usable with `pandoc -f json -t docx/pdf/epub/...`

### Quarto

- The Pandoc JSON AST, as for the Pandoc format, for Quarto's Pandoc-based pipeline
- Optionally wrapped in a `tbl-<id>` div for cross-references (`table_id` option)

## Binary Formats

### DOCX (Microsoft Word)

- Valid Office Open XML archive (ZIP)
- Table in `word/document.xml`
- Styles in `word/styles.xml`: Calibri 11pt with no space between paragraphs, the
  `Title` (16pt), `Subtitle` (12pt), `FootnoteText` and `SourceNote` (9pt) paragraph
  styles and the `TableGrid` table style, so the document's look can be changed by
  editing its styles in Word. A relative font size on the title or a note resolves
  against its paragraph style's size
- Horizontal merge via `<w:gridSpan>`, vertical via `<w:vMerge>`
- Bold, italic, color, size, font (`<w:rFonts>`), shading and alignment
- Table-wide single grid lines; a cell's own borders (`<w:tcBorders>`: solid, dashed,
  dotted, double) replace them on the sides it sets
- Vertical alignment via `<w:vAlign>`, on every piece of a vertically merged cell
- Column widths in `<w:tblGrid>` (dxa, 1/1440 inch), the table's width their sum.
  `%` and `fr` columns divide the table's width: `table_width`, else a 6in line (the
  document sets no page). When `table_width` is set and no column is `fr`, the
  columns without a width share what the others leave; otherwise each is 1.5in, as
  is an `fr` column the others leave no room for. `em` is 11pt. Every column is at
  least a dxa wide, and widths that would add up to more than the table's width can
  hold (about 38km) are scaled down to fit, in proportion

### XLSX (Microsoft Excel)

- SpreadsheetML format
- Cells preserve typed values, each shown as the table shows it:
  - Numbers stay numeric, with a number format read off the display (`0.0` for `76.0`,
    `#,##0` for `1,250`).
  - Dates, datetimes and times are date serials, with a date format read off the display
    (`yyyy\-mm\-dd` for `2024-03-15`, `mmm d\, yyyy` for `Mar 15, 2024`). Month and
    weekday names and AM/PM are English (the format pins en-US, so Excel shows them
    in English whatever its language), and literal separators are escaped (Excel
    would otherwise put its own date separator in place of `/`). The display's
    digits must all be the value's fields, and a time with fractions of a second
    must show them (to milliseconds). Dates before 1900-03-01 stay text: Excel
    counts a 1900-02-29 that never was.
  - Booleans are boolean cells when the display is `TRUE` or `FALSE` (in any case:
    Excel shows its own `TRUE` and `FALSE`).

  A typed cell whose display no format reproduces (`<0.001`, `yes`, `Q1 2024`, a
  footnote mark) stays text.
- Merge regions via `<mergeCells>`
- Styles in `xl/styles.xml` (fonts, fills, borders, number formats; a cell with no
  font of its own is in Calibri); rich text where a cell mixes formatting, in the
  shared-string table (apps such as Numbers ignore run formatting in inline strings)
- Cells with line breaks wrap, and rows are tall enough for their lines and font sizes
- Vertical alignment via the `vertical` attribute (Excel's own default is bottom)

### PPTX (Microsoft PowerPoint)

- DrawingML table (`<a:tbl>`) in a slide shape
- Grid-based spans with `gridSpan`/`rowSpan` attributes
- Text color, weight, slant, size and font (`<a:latin>`, `<a:ea>`, `<a:cs>`), cell
  fills and alignment
- Cell borders as `lnL`/`lnR`/`lnT`/`lnB` lines (solid, dashed, dotted, double)
- Vertical alignment via the cell's `anchor`
- Column widths in EMU, the table centered on the slide. `%` and `fr` columns divide
  the table's width: `table_width`, else the slide's text width (9in, as the title
  and notes). When `table_width` is set and no column is `fr`, the columns without a
  width share what the others leave; otherwise each is 1in, as is an `fr` column the
  others leave no room for. `em` is 18pt, PowerPoint's table text size. Widths that
  would add up to more than the table's frame can hold (about 60m) are scaled down
  to fit, in proportion
- A complete package (theme, master color map, notes size), so PowerPoint and Keynote
  open it
